newsitem.title: UK: UK monetary committee meets,markets on tenterhooks.
newsitem.headline: UK monetary committee meets,markets on tenterhooks.

text.p: Britains new monetary policy committee convened on Wednesday with an interest rate rise widely tipped to follow and markets on tenterhooks as a result.

The Bank of Englands committee, freed to set interest rates by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, will make its decision known at midday on Thursday. Nearly every investor and his dog expects a quarter-point rise, taking base rates to 6.75 percent.

A poll of 75 market participants across Europe by financial analysts 4CAST, found 67 expected the Banks monetary policy committee to raise rates on Thursday. Of those, 61 expected a quarter-point rise. Only six forecast a half-point increase.

U.K. markets acted like rabbits caught in the headlights ahead of the rate decision. By late morning, the FTSE-100 index of leading shares was just five points higher at 4,764. It shed more than 50 points on Tuesday, rattled by fears of a more aggressive rate rise.
The Financial Times newspaper said on Wednesday that a half-point tightening was needed to stop booming consumer spending in its tracks. It said a full-point rise might be better.
But the markets were not buying that story today. The September long gilt future was just 1/32 lower at 114-20 by 1015 GMT on Wednesday.
The September short sterling future was unchanged at 92.80. That is pricing in base rates at seven percent by the end of September but there are another two monetary meetings before then.
Peter Osler, analyst at GNI, said gilts would be little moved by a quarter-point hike. "I don't think the market will flinch at that."
Much as the Bank of England might wish to make a decisive interest rate move, it knows it risks propelling the pound higher and higher if it does.
UK exporters are struggling as the pound -- up more than 20 percent in 11 months -- inflates their prices. A hefty rate rise would worsen their pain.
Like the FTSE and gilts, sterling was consolidating on Wednesday, just below the six-year highs above 2.97 marks it set on Tuesday.

The main problem with a half-point rate rise is that it would send sterling spinning still higher, one dealer said. It would leave the markets believing the bears who see rates peaking at 8.0 to 8.5 percent.

The plight of exporters leaves the Bank facing a dilemma because consumer spending, fuelled by more than 30 billion pounds in windfall payments from building societies converting into banks, is booming.
Retail sales leapt 1.1 percent in May and on Wednesday electrical retailer Dixons Group Plc said sales were up 17 percent in the first nine weeks of its financial year, boosted by windfall cash.
Many economists say Britains new Chancellor of the Exchequer, Gordon Brown, missed an opportunity to take the heat out of high street spending in his first budget last week.
To hit the consumer sector with less than a billion pounds of fiscal tightening when it is getting about 35 billion from the building societies really is a drop in the ocean, the dealer said.
Inflation data on Tuesday hardly eased interest rate fears. Underlying RPI jumped to 2.7 percent in the year to June, above the government's 2.5 target.

On the other hand, figures released on Monday showed manufacturing output slumped 1.1 percent in May, the biggest one-month drop in four years -- the economy is, if anything, becoming more unbalanced, not less.

The Engineering Employers Federation added its voice to the chorus of hard-pressed manufacturers on Tuesday. It said engineering export orders plunged to their lowest level for three years in the second quarter, as the pounds strength bit.
But the Bank is likely to remain unmoved by those pleas, fulfilling its mandate to temper the inflation outlook two years out.
David Bloom, economist at HSBC James Capel, expects a 25 basis point rate rise. The Bank will take sterlings rise on board but will still go for a cautious increase.
